Chapter 14
First Hop Redundancy Protocol (HSRP)

This document replaces Chapter 14 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (2020), book pages 411 to 432. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objective, and marks every place where it adds to, corrects, or could not verify the book. It covers why hosts need a redundant default gateway, how FHRPs work, and HSRP in detail (MAC address, timers, roles, tracking, preemption, verification, load sharing, troubleshooting). Because Cisco's v2.0 outline now names VRRP as well, a short added section covers VRRP and GLBP.

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Learning objective (from the book). One exam objective is listed for this chapter: 3.5 Describe the purpose of first hop redundancy protocol.

Chapter goal. Build redundancy (and some load sharing) into the network using routers you may already own, by learning Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP). The book says the Cisco objectives cover little configuration, but verification and troubleshooting matter. BOOK
VERIFY

Verification note. Virtual MAC addresses, hex conversions, election and preemption results, timer maths, and lab addressing were calculated with a Python script (ch14_verify.py, in the build folder). Facts that could have changed were checked against Cisco documents and other sources; the Sources table at the end says which were official.
No command in this document was run on real Cisco equipment or in Packet Tracer. Outputs are illustrative and tagged CHECK .

The book teaches HSRP only; VRRP is added in this document. UPDATED Official Cisco source (v2.0 PDF).

Book pages 412 to 414.

The idea in plain words. A host has one default gateway setting, typed in by hand or given by DHCP. Most host operating systems cannot change how they route. If that gateway router dies, the routers on the network find another path, but nobody tells the host. The host keeps sending to the dead router. BOOK
Figure 14.1 in the book shows two routers on one subnet (10.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.2). Host 10.0.0.100 knows only 10.0.0.1. The second router is available but unused.
Proxy ARP: the old, accidental fix
Proxy ARP is on by default on Cisco router interfaces. It lets a host with no routing knowledge reach other networks. BOOK
- The host sends an ARP request for a destination IP address that is not on its subnet, as if the destination were local.
- A Proxy ARP router that can reach that destination answers with its own MAC address.
- The host sends the packets to that MAC address. The router forwards them to the real destination.
- If that router fails, the host keeps using the old MAC address from its ARP cache until the entry ages out.
- Then the host sends a new ARP request and the other router answers. Until that happens the host cannot send packets off its subnet. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

On pages 413 to 414 the book says that because packets go to a failed router "the packets will be sent to the other router". That sentence is muddled. What really happens is: the packets keep going to the dead router's MAC address until the ARP entry expires, and only then does the other router answer. Failover is slow because it depends on the ARP timeout. UPDATED ARP timeouts differ by operating system. CHECK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Proxy ARP was not designed as a gateway redundancy tool, and many designs turn it off. ADDED CHECK General knowledge, not verified in this session.
WHY THIS MATTERS
This slow, accidental failover is the problem FHRPs solve. They give the host one gateway that never changes and fail over in seconds or less.
Quick check: 14.1
Q1. Why does the host not learn about the failure of its gateway?
Answer: Routers update each other, not the hosts - hosts have a single configured gateway and usually do not run routing.
Q2. In Proxy ARP, whose MAC address does the router give to the host?
Answer: The router's own MAC address - the host thinks it is the MAC of the destination.
Q3. What decides how long a host keeps sending to a dead Proxy ARP router?
Answer: The ARP cache timeout on the host - the old entry must age out before a new ARP request is sent.
Book pages 414 to 416.

The idea in plain words. An FHRP makes several physical routers look like one logical router. The "first hop" is the first router a packet passes through, which is the default gateway. The group shares a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC address. Hosts use the virtual IP as their default gateway and learn the virtual MAC by ARP. They never know which physical router is forwarding. BOOK

The protocol decides which router is active (forwards traffic) and which is on standby. If the active router fails, the standby router starts using the virtual IP and MAC, so the change is transparent to the hosts (Figure 14.3). BOOK
The three FHRPs
| Protocol | Origin | How it works | Load sharing | Book comment (p. 416) |
| HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) | Cisco proprietary | One active router, others wait | Not true load balancing. Per VLAN only, by tricks. | Covered in detail in this chapter |
| VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) | Open standard | Almost identical to HSRP | Not load balanced | Said to be "not covered" now (see warning) |

| GLBP (Gateway Load Balancing Protocol) | Cisco proprietary | Several routers forward at once | True load balancing. Up to four routers in a group. Round-robin by default. | Not on the objectives, per the book |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book says "only one is covered on the CCNA objectives now". In v2.0 both HSRP and VRRP are named (objective 3.4). See the added VRRP and GLBP section later. UPDATED
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says on page 416 that HSRP lets you "buy up to eight routers" and keep seven as backup. On page 421 it says a group can have "up to 255" routers. These two numbers do not agree. I did not find an official limit, so do not memorize either. In practice most groups have two routers. UPDATED CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
An FHRP is not a routing protocol. It gives hosts a redundant default gateway. (Book review question 2.)
HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary. VRRP is a standard. (Book Exam Essentials.)
MEMORY TIP
The virtual router is just an IP address and a MAC address that move between real routers.
Quick check: 14.2
Q1. What do hosts use as their default gateway when an FHRP is running?
Answer: The virtual IP address - the physical addresses of the routers are not used by hosts.
Q2. Which FHRP is an open standard?
Answer: VRRP - HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary.
Q3. Which FHRP gives true load balancing?
Answer: GLBP - HSRP and VRRP use one forwarding router per group.
Q4. Why is failover transparent to hosts?
Answer: The standby router takes over the same virtual IP and MAC - the host's gateway setting and ARP entry stay valid.
Book pages 416 to 418.
The idea in plain words. HSRP is Cisco's FHRP. It runs on most (not all) Cisco routers and multilayer switches. Routers that run HSRP for one subnet form a standby group. The group has: BOOK
- an active router (forwards the traffic),
- a standby router (the backup),
- a virtual router (the shared IP and MAC), and
- any other routers on the subnet that are in the group.

Only the active router forwards traffic sent to the virtual router. The others wait, which the book calls "not very cost effective" (Figure 14.4). The active and standby routers talk using multicast Hello messages. The Hellos carry the information for the election and the failover. If the standby router stops hearing Hellos from the active router, it becomes active (Figure 14.5). BOOK
Who becomes active?
- The router with the highest priority wins. Default priority is 100. Range is 0 to 255.
- If priorities are equal, the router with the highest IP address on the HSRP interface wins. ADDED
- The election matters when routers start at the same time. If one router is already active, a new router does not take over unless preempt is configured (see 14.3.4).
VERIFY

The tie-break by highest IP address is not in the book. It comes from Cisco community material and a summary source. Cisco community posts also say that a standby router with equal priority but a higher IP does not preempt the active router, so the IP tie-break applies at election time. Do not rely on a tie in an exam answer. ADDED CHECK
HSRP version 1 and version 2
The book mentions versions 1 and 2 only in the troubleshooting part (page 429). They differ in several ways that you should know:
| Feature | HSRP version 1 (default) | HSRP version 2 |
| Hello multicast address | 224.0.0.2 | 224.0.0.102 |
| Transport | UDP port 1985 | UDP port 1985 |
| Group numbers | 0 to 255 | 0 to 4095 |
| Virtual MAC range | 0000.0C07.AC00 to 0000.0C07.ACFF | 0000.0C9F.F000 to 0000.0C9F.FFFF |
| Millisecond timers | Not advertised or learned | Advertised and learned |
| Changing the version | Each group reinitializes (it gets a new virtual MAC) | Same |
Version 1 is the default on Cisco IOS. ADDED Official Cisco sources (HSRP configuration guides). The book's own table of versions is missing, so memorize this one.
EXAM CRITICAL
Default priority 100. Range 0 to 255. Highest priority is active. (Book review questions 1, 6, 8.)
Only one active router and one standby router per group (other routers wait).
Preempt is off by default. The first router up stays active.
VERIFY
HSRP is described in RFC 2281 (informational), according to a secondary source. I did not open the RFC. CHECK
Quick check: 14.3
Q1. How do the active and standby routers talk to each other?
Answer: Multicast Hello messages - they carry election information and tell the standby router the active router is alive.
Q2. Both routers start at the same time with priority 100. Router A is 10.1.1.1 and Router B is 10.1.1.2. Who becomes active?
Answer: Router B - equal priority, so the higher IP address wins the election. CHECK
Q3. What is the HSRP version 1 Hello destination?
Answer: 224.0.0.2, UDP port 1985 - version 2 uses 224.0.0.102.
Q4. How many routers forward traffic for the virtual router in one HSRP group?
Answer: One, the active router - the others are standby or just listening.
14.3.1 Virtual MAC Address

Book pages 418 to 419. The virtual IP address is easy: it is an unused IP address on the same subnet as the hosts. The virtual MAC address is a made-up MAC address built from fixed and variable parts. BOOK
| Bits | Example | Meaning |
| First 24 bits | 0000.0c | Vendor ID (OUI). Here it is Cisco. |
| Next 16 bits | 07.ac | The well-known HSRP ID. It means "this is an HSRP address". |
| Last 8 bits | 0a | The HSRP group number in hexadecimal (10 decimal = 0a) |
Example: 0000.0c07.ac0a is the virtual MAC address of HSRP group 10 (version 1). You will see the virtual IP and virtual MAC pair in the ARP cache of the routers in the group. BOOK
Decimal to hex for the last byte (version 1)
| Group (decimal) | Hex | Virtual MAC, version 1 | Virtual MAC, version 2 ADDED |
All values were calculated by the script. Version 2 uses 12 bits for the group number, so the group can be up to 4095 (0000.0c9f.ffff). ADDED Official Cisco source.
MEMORY TIP
To convert a group number: divide by 16. The quotient is the first hex digit and the remainder is the second. Group 20 = 1 x 16 + 4 = 14. Group 100 = 6 x 16 + 4 = 64.
EXAM CRITICAL
If you see 0000.0c07.acXX in an ARP table or show standby output, it is an HSRP version 1 virtual MAC. The last two digits are the group in hex. The book's Exam Essentials repeats this example.
Quick check: 14.3.1
Q1. What group number is 0000.0c07.ac0a?
Answer: Group 10 - 0a in hex is 10 in decimal.
Q2. Write the version 1 virtual MAC for group 20.
Answer: 0000.0c07.ac14 - 20 = 0x14 (checked by script).
Q3. Which part of the virtual MAC tells you it is an HSRP address?
Answer: 07.ac (the well-known HSRP ID) - the OUI 0000.0c only says Cisco.
14.3.2 HSRP Timers
Book pages 419 to 421. Four timers keep the group working and let the standby router take over. BOOK
| Timer | Default | What it does |
| Hello | 3 seconds | How often each router sends Hello messages that state its role. |
| Hold | 10 seconds | How long the standby router waits without hearing the active router before it decides the active router is gone. |
| Active | Follows the hold time in the Hello | Watches the active router. It is reset each time a Hello arrives from the active router. |
| Standby | Follows the hold time in the Hello | Watches the standby router. It is reset each time a Hello arrives from the standby router. |
The book recommends keeping the hold time at about three times the hello time, so a short break in communication does not trigger a takeover. If you lower one timer, lower the other too. BOOK
Sub-second timers
In a sidebar (pages 420 to 421) the book says 10 seconds is "a lifetime" and shows timers of 200 ms (hello) and 700 ms (hold):
Book example, command in correct case BOOK
Router(config-if)# standby 1 timers msec 200 msec 700
| Setting | Hello | Hold | Worst-case wait before takeover |
| Default | 3 s | 10 s | About 10 s |
| Book sidebar | 200 ms | 700 ms | About 0.7 s (about 14 times faster, checked by script) |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says these timers "almost ensure" no packet is lost. That is too strong. Traffic in flight can still be lost, and other parts of the network (such as the routing back to the LAN) also take time. UPDATED

Cisco says version 1 does not advertise or learn millisecond timers; version 2 does. So for sub-second timers use standby version 2 and set the same timers on every router in the group. The book does not mention this. UPDATED Official Cisco source.
WARNING
Very short timers on a busy or unstable network can cause the active role to flap. Test any change. ADDED CHECK
Quick check: 14.3.2
Q1. What are the default HSRP hello and hold times?
Answer: 3 seconds and 10 seconds - the hold time is about three times the hello time.
Q2. Which timer makes the standby router decide the active router is gone?
Answer: The hold timer - it counts the time without a Hello from the active router.
Q3. To use millisecond timers that all routers learn, which HSRP version do you need?
Answer: Version 2 - version 1 does not advertise or learn millisecond timers.
Book pages 421 to 422. Each router in the standby group has a role. BOOK
| Role | What it is and does |
| Virtual router | Not a physical device. It is a role held by the active router: a separate IP address and MAC address that packets are sent to. |

| Active router | The physical router that receives packets sent to the virtual router and routes them onward. It accepts packets sent to the virtual MAC and to its own MAC. It also answers ARP requests for the virtual IP. |
| Standby router | The backup. It watches the group and takes over quickly if the active router fails or stops talking. Active and standby routers both send Hello messages. |

| Other routers | Extra members of the group. They watch the Hellos to make sure an active and a standby router exist. They forward only packets addressed to their own IP, and never forward packets for the virtual router unless they become active or standby. |
VERIFY

The book says other routers send "speak" messages based on the hello interval. This is unclear: routers that are only listening do not normally send Hellos. I could not confirm this and I would not rely on it. Also, the book says a group can hold "up to 255" other routers, which conflicts with the "eight" on page 416 (see 14.2). CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
Know the three main roles: virtual router, active router, standby router. A router answering the ARP request for the virtual IP is the active router.
Interface Tracking (book heading on page 422, not in the table of contents)

The idea in plain words. HSRP protects the LAN side. But what if the active router's link to the Internet or the core fails? The active router would still be active on the LAN and would send the hosts' traffic into a dead end. Interface tracking solves this. The router watches an outside interface. If it goes down, the router lowers its own priority, so the standby router can take over (Figure 14.7). BOOK

The book says the default priority is 100, a higher priority wins, and a tracked interface that goes down decrements the priority. It does not show the command, the default decrement, or what else must be configured. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Default decrement is 10. You can change it. ADDED Official Cisco source.

The standby router must have preempt. Lowering the active router's priority only makes the standby router take over if the standby router is configured to preempt. ADDED Official Cisco source (the standby preempt and standby track document).

Make the decrement big enough. If the active router has priority 110 and the decrement is 10, its priority becomes 100, which equals the standby router's priority. A tie does not cause a takeover on its own. Use a decrement that pushes the priority below the standby router's priority (for example decrement 20: 110 - 20 = 90). ADDED CHECK tie behavior.
Illustrative tracking configuration on the active router (object tracking) ADDED CHECK
R1(config)# track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 line-protocol
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
R1(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track 1 decrement 20
- track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 line-protocol: creates tracking object 1 that watches the uplink.
- standby 1 priority 110: this router normally wins the election.
- standby 1 preempt: lets the router take the active role back when it can.
- standby 1 track 1 decrement 20: if object 1 goes down, lower the priority by 20 (110 to 90).

Older IOS versions also accept a direct form: standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/1 20. Which form you need depends on your software version. CHECK Remember that the standby router (R2) also needs standby 1 preempt.
Quick check: 14.3.3
Q1. Which router answers ARP requests for the virtual IP address?
Answer: The active router - it owns the virtual IP and MAC at that moment.
Q2. What does interface tracking do?
Answer: It lowers the router's HSRP priority when a tracked interface goes down - so the standby router can become active.
Q3. R1 has priority 110, R2 has 100. R1 tracks its uplink with decrement 20. R2 has preempt. The uplink fails. Who is active?
Answer: R2 - R1 drops to 90, which is below R2's 100, and R2 can preempt.
Q4. Same as above but R2 has no preempt. Who is active?
Answer: R1 stays active - without preempt the standby router does not take over because of a priority change. CHECK on hardware.
14.3.4 Configuring and Verifying HSRP
Book pages 423 to 428. The book uses two routers (HSRP1 and HSRP2) on subnet 10.1.1.0/24 with virtual IP 10.1.1.10 (Figure 14.8). The only command you really need is: BOOK
Minimum HSRP configuration BOOK
Router(config-if)# standby GROUP ip VIRTUAL-IP
The book names the group, and sets HSRP1's priority to 110 so it wins the election. HSRP2 keeps the default 100.
Book example (commands only) BOOK
HSRP1(config)# interface fa0/0
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 name HSRP_Test
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
HSRP2(config)# interface fa0/0
HSRP2(config-if)# standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10
HSRP2(config-if)# standby 1 name HSRP_Test
- standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10: enable HSRP group 1 with virtual IP 10.1.1.10. The group number must match on all routers, and so must the virtual IP.
- standby 1 name HSRP_Test: optional. For administration only.
- standby 1 priority 110: raises HSRP1's priority above the default 100, so it wins the election.
- HSRP2 needs only the first command. It becomes standby because its priority is lower.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
The book points out that priority only decides the winner if both routers come up at the same time. If HSRP2 comes up first, it becomes active regardless of priority, because preempt is not on. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book's console line after setting the priority reads "Standby -> Active110" (page 424). That is a garbled line: the state message is "Standby -> Active" and the 110 is a typing mix-up. UPDATED
The standby command options (page 423 to 424)
| Option | Meaning |
| group number | 0 to 255 (version 1) |
| ip | Enable HSRP and set the virtual IP address |
| priority | Priority level (default 100) |
| preempt | Overthrow a lower-priority active router |
| timers | Hello and hold timers |
| track | Priority tracking |
| name | Redundancy name |
| version | HSRP version 1 or 2 |
| authentication, delay, mac-address, redirect, use-bia | Other options. The book does not use them. |
Preemption

The idea in plain words. Without preempt, the router that became active first stays active, even if a router with a higher priority comes up later. Preemption lets the higher-priority router take over. It is the only way to force a new election when no device has failed. BOOK
Book example, with the command spelled correctly BOOK
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
HSRP1(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
COMMON MISTAKE
The book types the command as standby 1 prempt on page 425. That is a spelling error and IOS will reject it. The correct command is standby 1 preempt. UPDATED
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
You can delay the takeover, to let routing settle after a reboot: standby 1 preempt delay minimum 60. ADDED CHECK syntax.
EXAM CRITICAL
Book review question 8: HSRP1 (priority 120) reboots; HSRP2 (default) became active. When HSRP1 comes back it becomes active only if it is configured to preempt. Otherwise HSRP2 stays active.
Book review question 1 asks for the default priority: 100.

| Line | What it tells you |
| GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1 | The interface and the HSRP group number. The group must match on both routers. |
| State is Active | This router is the active router. |

Illustrative show standby brief on both routers CHECK
R1# show standby brief
P indicates configured to preempt.
Interface Grp Pri P State Active Standby Virtual IP
R2# show standby brief
Interface Grp Pri P State Active Standby Virtual IP
- Grp: group number. Pri: this router's priority. P: a P means the router is configured to preempt (blank = no preempt).
- State: Active or Standby for this router. Active and Standby columns: the IP of that router, or local if it is this router.
- Virtual IP: the shared gateway address.
EXAM CRITICAL

The book says: "Notice the group number in each output, it's a key troubleshooting spot." Each router must be in the same group, with the same virtual IP, or HSRP will not work as one virtual router. Review question 5: show standby shows the status of the HSRP groups.
HSRP states (Table 14.1)
| State | Meaning |
| Init | The start state. HSRP is not running yet. Entered after a configuration change or when the interface first comes up. |
| Learn | The router does not yet know the virtual IP and has not heard from the active router. It waits. |
| Listen | The router knows the virtual IP, but it is neither active nor standby. It listens for Hellos. |
| Speak | The router sends Hellos and takes part in the election. It cannot be in this state without knowing the virtual IP. |
| Standby | The next candidate to be active. It sends Hellos. At most one router per group is in this state. |
| Active | The router forwards packets sent to the virtual MAC and sends Hellos. At most one router per group is in this state. |
A router normally starts in Init, then moves through Listen and Speak to Standby or Active. The console messages in the book show this: "Speak -> Standby" and "Standby -> Active". BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

On page 426 the book shuts down the interface and sees "Active -> Init". It says Init means the router is "trying to initialize with a peer". That contradicts the book's own Table 14.1, which says Init means HSRP is not running yet. Use the table. Also, the console message names Ethernet0/0 while the example router uses FastEthernet0/0, so the book's output is from a different setup. UPDATED
EXAM CRITICAL
Book review question 3: INIT and ACTIVE are HSRP states. ESTABLISHED and IDLE are not.
debug standby
The book shows debug standby output while an interface comes up. It prints each HSRP event (MAC set, state change, ARP reload). It is a good way to watch HSRP work in a lab. BOOK
WARNING
debug commands use CPU and flood the screen. Use them briefly in a lab, then turn them off with undebug all. ADDED
HSRP load balancing (page 427 to 428, Figure 14.9)

The idea in plain words. HSRP is not true load balancing, because only one router is active per group. But you can run two groups on the same pair of routers. One group has router A active and the other group has router B active. Hosts in VLAN 10 use group 10's virtual IP, and hosts in VLAN 20 use group 20's. Both routers carry traffic. In the book's example the links are trunks and each router uses subinterfaces (router on a stick). BOOK
| VLAN | HSRP group | Active router | Standby router |
| 10 | 10 | R1 (higher priority) | R2 |

Many networks now use Layer 3 switches with SVIs instead of router on a stick, and run HSRP on the SVIs. The idea is the same. The book only shows router on a stick. ADDED CHECK
WHY THIS MATTERS
The book says load sharing with HSRP "is the topic of an objective". Remember the trick: different groups, different active routers per VLAN. It is not true load balancing. GLBP does that.
HSRP troubleshooting (pages 428 to 429)
The book says troubleshooting is the Cisco objective "hotspot". Start with show standby. The book lists three misconfigurations: BOOK
| Misconfiguration | What happens (book) | How to see it |

| Different virtual IPs on the peers | Console messages appear. If the active router fails, the standby router takes over with a virtual IP that is different from the hosts' gateway. Hosts stop working. | show standby on both routers: compare the virtual IP |
| Different groups on the peers | Both routers become active, with duplicate IP address warnings. | show standby brief: both show Active, group numbers differ CHECK |

| Different versions, or blocked ports | Version mismatch: both become active, with duplicate IP warnings. Blocked Hellos: the peers never see each other, so there is no redundancy. | show standby (version line). Check ACLs for the HSRP multicast and UDP 1985. |
In version 1 Hellos go to 224.0.0.2, UDP port 1985. In version 2 they go to 224.0.0.102, UDP port 1985. These addresses and the port must be permitted in inbound access lists. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Other causes: the routers are not in the same subnet or VLAN, a Layer 2 problem blocks the Hellos, or authentication keys do not match. ADDED CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's Summary (page 429) says the chapter began "with a talk about how to mitigate security threats at the access layer and also discussed external authentication". That describes Chapter 13, not this chapter. It is a copy and paste error. UPDATED
Quick check: 14.3.4
Q1. Which command enables HSRP group 1 with the virtual IP 10.1.1.10?
Answer: standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10 - it is the one mandatory HSRP command.
Q2. Which command shows the HSRP status of all groups?
Answer: show standby (or show standby brief) - there is no show hsrp.
Q3. In show standby brief, what does the P column mean?
Answer: The router is configured to preempt - blank means no preempt.
Q4. A higher-priority router comes back up but does not become active. What is missing?
Answer: standby 1 preempt - without preempt the current active router stays active.
Q5. HSRP state that means the interface just came up and HSRP is not running yet?
Answer: Init - from Table 14.1.
Q6. How can you share traffic between two HSRP routers?
Answer: Two groups, with a different active router for each VLAN - this is load sharing, not true load balancing.

sections.title: Added: VRRP and GLBP Compared with HSRP

content.text: ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

This whole section is not in the book chapter. The book mentions VRRP and GLBP in two short paragraphs. Cisco's v2.0 objective 3.4 names VRRP and asks you to interpret the operational status of HSRP and VRRP. ADDED
| Feature | HSRP | VRRP | GLBP |
| Standard | Cisco proprietary | Open standard (RFC 5798 for VRRPv3) | Cisco proprietary |
| Roles | Active, Standby | Master, Backup | AVG (one router), AVFs (up to 4 forwarders) |
| Traffic | One active router per group | One master per group | All forwarders share traffic (per host) |
| Hello / advertisement | Hello 3 s, hold 10 s | Advertisement 1 s, master-down time about 3 times that plus a skew | Hello 3 s, hold 10 s |
| Multicast and transport | 224.0.0.2 (v1) or 224.0.0.102 (v2), UDP 1985 | 224.0.0.18, IP protocol 112 (not UDP) | Not covered in this chapter |
| Virtual MAC | 0000.0c07.acXX (v1), 0000.0c9f.fXXX (v2) | 0000.5e00.01XX (XX = group in hex) | Different virtual MAC per forwarder |
| Default priority | 100 (0 to 255) | 100 (1 to 254; 255 = the router that owns the virtual IP) | 100 |
| Preempt by default | No | Yes | No |

VRRP, HSRP, and GLBP table sources: Cisco Press summary (origin, roles, load sharing), the book (HSRP, GLBP details), Cisco-hosted VRRP output (virtual MAC and preemption enabled), and secondary VRRP summaries (multicast, protocol 112, default timers, priority 255 owner). The GLBP row is from the book and a secondary summary. CHECK
VRRP master-down time

A backup router decides the master is gone after 3 x advertisement interval + skew time, where skew = (256 - priority) � 256 x advertisement interval. With priority 100 and a 1 second advertisement, that is 3 + 0.609 = 3.609 seconds (calculated by script; a published example with priority 50 shows about 3.8 seconds, which also matches the formula). ADDED CHECK
VRRP configuration (illustrative)
Classic IOS style (VRRPv2) ADDED CHECK
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# vrrp 1 ip 192.168.10.1
R1(config-if)# vrrp 1 priority 110
Newer IOS XE style (VRRPv3) ADDED CHECK
R1(config)# fhrp version vrrp v3
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# vrrp 1 address-family ipv4
R1(config-if-vrrp)# address 192.168.10.1 primary
R1(config-if-vrrp)# priority 110
Which style you must use depends on the software version. VRRP preempts by default, so you do not need a preempt command. CHECK
Reading the output (objective 3.4)
Illustrative outputs CHECK
R1# show standby brief
P indicates configured to preempt.
Interface Grp Pri P State Active Standby Virtual IP
R2# show vrrp brief
Interface Grp Pri Time Own Pre State Master addr Group addr
Q1. In the HSRP output, which router is forwarding traffic for 192.168.10.1?
Answer: R1, because its state is Active and the Active column says local - R1 shows Active and local.
Q2. Is R1 configured to take back the active role if it loses it and recovers?
Answer: Yes - the P in the output means preempt is configured.
Q3. In the VRRP output, what is R2's role and who is the master?
Answer: R2 is a Backup; the master is 192.168.10.2 - the State column and the Master addr column.
Q4. What does Pre Y mean in the VRRP output?
Answer: Preemption is on - this is the VRRP default. CHECK column layout on your software.
GLBP in two lines

GLBP is Cisco proprietary and is the only one of the three that is true load balancing. One router (the AVG) answers ARP and hands out different virtual MACs so that hosts use different routers. The book says it supports a maximum of four routers in a group and uses round robin by default. BOOK GLBP is not named in v2.0 objective 3.4.

content.text: VERIFY

Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware, on IOS XE, or in Packet Tracer. All commands and outputs that were not directly confirmed from a Cisco document are tagged CHECK . Tracker rows in Notion were not updated: there was no Notion tool in this chat.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
The chapter points to bonus labs on the author's website (page 412) but has no labs in the chapter pages (411 to 432). The labs below are new. ADDED

Use Cisco Packet Tracer (three routers, one switch, two PCs, one server). All expected results are CHECK : nothing here was run in Packet Tracer or on real equipment, and the simulator may not support every HSRP feature (for example tracking or version 2).
| Device | Interface | Address | Role |
| R1 | G0/0 | 192.168.10.2/24 | LAN side, HSRP member (will be active) |
| R1 | G0/1 | 10.0.13.1/30 | Link to R3 (uplink, tracked in Lab 4) |
| R2 | G0/0 | 192.168.10.3/24 | LAN side, HSRP member (will be standby) |
| R3 ("core / Internet") | G0/0, G0/1, G0/2 | 10.0.13.2/30, 10.0.23.2/30, 192.0.2.1/24 | Connects both gateways and the server |
| Virtual router | (HSRP) | 192.168.10.1 | Gateway for the PCs |
Routes CHECK

Script check: all LAN addresses are in 192.168.10.0/24 and unique, both links are valid /30 networks with .1 and .2 in the same subnet, and nothing overlaps. R3 sends return traffic for the LAN through R2 only, so replies may come back by a different router than the one that forwarded the request. That works here, but a real network would use a routing protocol so R3 learns the LAN from both routers. ADDED
Q1. Write the version 1 and version 2 virtual MAC addresses for group 100.
Answer: 0000.0c07.ac64 and 0000.0c9f.f064 - 100 = 0x64 (checked by script).
Q2. R1 priority 100, IP 10.1.1.1. R2 priority 100, IP 10.1.1.2. Both boot together. Who is active?
Answer: R2 - equal priority, higher IP wins the election. CHECK
Q3. R2 (100) is active. R1 (110) boots later with no preempt. Who is active? What if R1 has preempt?
Answer: R2 stays active. With preempt, R1 becomes active - preempt lets a higher priority take over.
Configure IP addresses on all interfaces, add the routes above, and set the PCs' gateway to R1's real address, 192.168.10.2.

Test: ping 192.0.2.10 from PC1. Expected result: it works. Now shut R1's LAN interface (interface g0/0, shutdown) and ping again. Expected result: it fails, even though R2 is healthy, because the PC only knows R1. This is the problem from 14.1. CHECK
Undo the shutdown, then change the PCs' gateway to 192.168.10.1 (the virtual IP) before Lab 2.
Configuration CHECK
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1
R1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
R1(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
R2(config)# interface g0/0
R2(config-if)# standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1
- standby 1 ip 192.168.10.1: group 1 with virtual IP 192.168.10.1. Same group and same virtual IP on both routers.
- standby 1 priority 110: R1 wins the election. R2 keeps the default 100.
- standby 1 preempt: R1 takes the active role back when it returns.

Verify: show standby brief on both routers. Expected result: R1 is Active with priority 110 and a P. R2 is Standby with priority 100. The Virtual IP column shows 192.168.10.1. On a PC, ping the server, then look at the ARP table: 192.168.10.1 should map to 0000.0c07.ac01. CHECK

Failover test: start a continuous ping from PC1 to 192.0.2.10 (ping -t on Windows-like PCs). Shut R1's g0/0. Expected result: a few lost replies, then it works again through R2. show standby brief on R2 shows Active. With the default timers the pause can be up to about 10 seconds. Run no shutdown on R1: R1 should become Active again because it has preempt. CHECK

Part A, no preempt. On R1 run no standby 1 preempt. Shut and re-enable R1's g0/0. Expected result: R2 became Active during the outage and stays Active after R1 returns, even though R1 has the higher priority. Put standby 1 preempt back and watch R1 take over. CHECK
Part B, faster timers. On both routers:
Both routers CHECK
R1(config-if)# standby version 2
R1(config-if)# standby 1 timers msec 200 msec 700
R2(config-if)# standby version 2
R2(config-if)# standby 1 timers msec 200 msec 700
- standby version 2: version 2 advertises and learns millisecond timers. The group reinitializes because the virtual MAC changes.
- standby 1 timers msec 200 msec 700: hello 200 ms, hold 700 ms.

Expected result: show standby shows version 2 and a virtual MAC of 0000.0c9f.f001. Repeat the failover test from Lab 2. The pause should be shorter. Compare the number of lost replies. CHECK Return to the defaults afterward with no standby 1 timers on both routers.
Configuration CHECK
R1(config)# track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 line-protocol
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track 1 decrement 20
R2(config)# interface g0/0
R2(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
- track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 line-protocol: watch R1's uplink to R3.
- standby 1 track 1 decrement 20: if the uplink goes down, drop R1's priority from 110 to 90.
- standby 1 preempt on R2: the standby router must preempt to take over when R1's priority falls.

Test: start a continuous ping from PC1. Shut R1's g0/1. Expected result: show standby on R1 shows priority 90 and Track object 1 state Down. R2 becomes Active and the ping keeps working (R1's LAN side was healthy but its uplink was dead). no shutdown on g0/1: R1's priority returns to 110 and R1 takes the role back. CHECK

Extra experiment: change the decrement to 10 (110 - 10 = 100, equal to R2). Repeat the test and note whether R2 takes over. Cisco community posts say an equal priority does not cause preemption, so I expect R1 to stay active. Record what you actually saw. CHECK
VERIFY
If your simulator does not accept the track command, skip this lab, or use the older direct form standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/1 20 if it is accepted. Write down what happened.
| Fault | Expected symptom | How to find it | Fix |
| R2 uses virtual IP 192.168.10.100 instead of .1 | Console messages. If R1 fails, hosts lose their gateway. | show standby on both: compare the virtual IP | Use the same virtual IP |
| R2 uses group 2 instead of group 1 | Both routers show Active. Duplicate IP warnings. | show standby brief: group numbers differ | Use the same group |
| R2 uses standby version 2 and R1 does not | Both Active. Duplicate IP warnings. | show standby: v1 and v2 | Same version on both |
| Inbound ACL on R2's g0/0 denies UDP 1985 | R2 never hears R1, so both are Active | show access-lists; Hellos missing | Permit 224.0.0.2 and UDP 1985 |
| R1 has no preempt and was rebooted | R2 stays Active | show standby brief: no P | Add standby 1 preempt |
| R1 priority lowered to 90 | R2 becomes Active | Priority column | Restore priority 110 |

Replace HSRP with VRRP on both routers using the commands from the added VRRP section, on a real IOS or virtual IOS XE lab (not necessarily Packet Tracer, which may not support VRRP). Check show vrrp brief. Expected result: R1 (priority 110) is Master, R2 is Backup, and no preempt command is needed. Compare the virtual MAC (0000.5e00.0101) with HSRP's. CHECK

content.text: Q1 What group number is 0000.0c07.ac0a?
Answer: Group 10 - 0a in hex is 10 in decimal.
Q2 Write the version 1 virtual MAC for group 20.
Answer: 0000.0c07.ac14 - 20 = 0x14 (checked by script).
Q3 Which part of the virtual MAC tells you it is an HSRP address?
Answer: 07.ac (the well-known HSRP ID) - the OUI 0000.0c only says Cisco.
Q1 What are the default HSRP hello and hold times?
Answer: 3 seconds and 10 seconds - the hold time is about three times the hello time.
Q2 Which timer makes the standby router decide the active router is gone?
Answer: The hold timer - it counts the time without a Hello from the active router.
Q3 To use millisecond timers that all routers learn, which HSRP version do you need?
Answer: Version 2 - version 1 does not advertise or learn millisecond timers.
Q1 Which router answers ARP requests for the virtual IP address?
Answer: The active router - it owns the virtual IP and MAC at that moment.
Q2 What does interface tracking do?
Answer: It lowers the router's HSRP priority when a tracked interface goes down - so the standby router can become active.
Q3 R1 has priority 110, R2 has 100. R1 tracks its uplink with decrement 20. R2 has preempt. The uplink fails. Who is active?
Answer: R2 - R1 drops to 90, which is below R2's 100, and R2 can preempt.
Q4 Same as above but R2 has no preempt. Who is active?
Answer: R1 stays active - without preempt the standby router does not take over because of a priority change. CHECK on hardware.
Q1 Which command enables HSRP group 1 with the virtual IP 10.1.1.10?
Answer: standby 1 ip 10.1.1.10 - it is the one mandatory HSRP command.
Q2 Which command shows the HSRP status of all groups?
Answer: show standby (or show standby brief) - there is no show hsrp.
Q3 In show standby brief, what does the P column mean?
Answer: The router is configured to preempt - blank means no preempt.
Q4 A higher-priority router comes back up but does not become active. What is missing?
Answer: standby 1 preempt - without preempt the current active router stays active.
Q5 HSRP state that means the interface just came up and HSRP is not running yet?
Answer: Init - from Table 14.1.
Q6 How can you share traffic between two HSRP routers?
Answer: Two groups, with a different active router for each VLAN - this is load sharing, not true load balancing.
